text: A written report and a presentation serve different purposes, even when they cover the same work. This lesson is about building the presentation version of your capstone — for a technical audience that could ask you hard questions about your methods.

This lesson covers how a technical presentation's structure differs from the written report's, a slide-by-slide outline for a ten to fifteen minute capstone presentation, how to anticipate the hard technical questions your specific results invite, and common presentation mistakes that undercut strong underlying work.

A report can be read at the reader's own pace; a presentation is linear and time-boxed, so lead with the question and headline finding rather than building up to a conclusion. The outline: title and one-sentence question, brief motivation, then your hypothesis stated clearly before showing any results — this lets the audience judge your results against your own stated prediction. Then method at the right altitude, your main results with actual numbers, a limitations slide you do not rush, a bounded conclusion, and backup slides presented only if asked.

Before presenting, list the three hardest questions a skeptical technical reviewer could ask. For the running example: how do you know the calibration-window gap, not something else, explains the original discrepancy — answer, the same-window retry reversed the pattern, which is direct evidence. Why only three and five qubits, not a denser sweep — answer, a time and queue-budget scoping decision, stated honestly. Is 1,024 shots enough to trust these numbers — answer, reference your significance check directly.

In the worked outline, the hypothesis slide states the exact three-versus-five-qubit relative-magnitude claim, and the results slide shows both the original and corrected comparisons side by side, since that comparison is part of the finding — hiding the confounded run would actually make the presentation less credible, not more polished. Common mistakes include spending too much time on methods detail that belongs in backup slides, and presenting only the clean final result while omitting the confound-and-correction story, often the most interesting part of the actual research process.

Next lesson takes the same result and tells it to a hiring manager or a general audience — not a dumbed-down version of the technical talk, but a genuinely different structure built around what a non-specialist actually needs to trust.
